docs.title: Hello!
docs.text: I am a Ph.D. Candidate in Accounting at IESE Business School, expected to complete my Ph.D. in 2027. My research examines how stakeholder, labor-market, and technological environments shape corporate disclosure and information strategies. I combine archival empirical methods with large-scale textual analysis, computational data collection, and machine-learning and natural-language-processing techniques.

docs.title: Same Interdependent Risk, Different Valuation: How Risk Representation Shapes Ecosystem Investment Decisions
docs.text:
Shiyao Bao, Jiamin Zhao, En Yang, Llewellyn D. W. Thomas, Hansjörg Neth, Jan K. Woike, and Sebastian Hafenbrädl

Journal of Management Scientific Reports, 4(4), 414-443, 2026.

docs.title: Public Activism and Labor-related Corporate Disclosure
docs.text:
Authorship: Single-authored

Abstract

This paper examines how the surrounding public environment shapes labor-related corporate disclosure. Greater non-firm-specific labor public activism around corporate headquarters is associated with less discussion of current labor-related operating conditions relative to talent-management information in subsequent earnings calls. The findings show that firms adjust disclosure to changes in the surrounding public environment even when the underlying activism does not directly target the firm.

Award: The Sue Hrasky Best PhD Paper Prize, BAFA, 2026.

Selected presentations: EAA Doctoral Colloquium 2026; IESE Seminar 2026; BAFA Annual Conference 2026; JIAR Annual Conference 2026; University of Zurich DAR Workshop 2025.

docs.title: Mapping Corporate Digital Information-Access Policies: Evidence from Web Access Directives
docs.text:
Coauthors: Long Cheng and Igor Kadach

Status: Manuscript in preparation

Abstract

This paper constructs a novel historical measure of corporate information-access policies from 2001 to 2024. We document how public firms govern automated access to information on their websites, characterize the long-run evolution and composition of these policies, and validate the measure using externally documented changes in web-access rules. The evidence reveals a previously underexplored dimension of corporate information policy: firms not only decide what information to make public, but also govern the scope and terms of automated access to that information.

docs.title: Stakeholder Pressure and the Supply of Corporate Information
docs.text:
Authorship: Single-authored

Abstract

This paper examines how firms adjust disclosure when directly targeted by stakeholder pressure. Labor targeting is associated with less discussion of labor operating conditions, whereas environmental targeting is associated with more climate-transition discussion. Employee reviews further suggest that labor targeting is accompanied by greater employee-generated discussion of labor issues. The findings highlight how stakeholder pressure can elicit different information responses from managers and employees, reshaping the composition and sources of corporate information.

docs.title: Protecting Information Without Disclosing Less: Governing the Downstream Use of Corporate Information
docs.text:
Coauthor: Long Cheng

Abstract

This project examines whether firms can protect the proprietary value of information without reducing public disclosure. Using the emergence of generative-AI information-use controls, we study a distinct margin of corporate information policy: firms' ability to govern downstream uses of information that remains publicly available. Preliminary evidence shows substantial heterogeneity in firms' adoption of AI-related restrictions, with adoption concentrated among firms that previously differentiated among automated agents.
